sources.title: Sophie Legrand, The emergence of the Karasuk culture, Antiquity
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis of the Minusinsk Basin setting, Karasuk emergence, metallurgy, pastoralism and Tagar succession.

sources.title: Svyatko and colleagues, New radiocarbon dates and a review of the chronology of prehistoric populations from the Minusinsk Basin
sources.note: Direct dates, competing archaeological chronologies, Classic and Kamenniy Log phases, sample caveats and ninth-century transition.

sources.title: Polyakov and colleagues, Current state of the chronology for the palaeometal period of the Minusinsk basins
sources.note: Modern review emphasizing difficult absolute chronology and the overly broad traditional Late Bronze Age Karasuk concept.

sources.title: Svyatko and colleagues, A lack of freshwater reservoir effects in human radiocarbon dates in the Minusinsk Basin
sources.note: Paired dating, river reservoir-effect tests, fifteenth- to ninth-century chronology and variable millet and fish signals.

sources.title: Svyatko and colleagues, Millet consumption in Siberia prior to the mid-second millennium BC?
sources.note: Review correcting earlier dates and linking reliable Late Bronze Age millet evidence, tools and changing contacts without assuming one uniform diet.

sources.title: History of Civilizations of Central Asia, Volume I, pastoral and nomadic tribes chapter
sources.note: UNESCO scholarly synthesis of Karasuk graves, pottery, bronze casting, livestock, horse gear, settlements and regional transition.

sources.title: Khakass National Museum, Karasuk culture: ancient bronze founders
sources.note: Regional museum account of the culture name, Torgazhaks settlement, house forms, furnaces, pottery, burials and engraved pebbles.

sources.title: Monumental Myopia: bringing the later prehistoric settlements of southern Siberia into focus, Antiquity
sources.note: Peer-reviewed survey showing how conspicuous monuments and cemeteries can bias reconstructions while settlements remain harder to locate.

sources.title: Katheryn Linduff and Karen Rubinson, Archaeology and Gender in the Russian Far East
sources.note: Academic volume summarizing analysis of about four hundred sexed Karasuk graves, cemetery clusters, family organization and gendered grave goods.

sources.title: Smithsonian Libraries, Are All Warriors Male? Gender Roles on the Ancient Eurasian Steppe
sources.note: Museum-library record for the scholarly volume containing the Karasuk gender and mortuary analysis used with explicit burial-to-life cautions.

sources.title: Marchenko and colleagues, Karasuk People in the Aley Steppe
sources.note: Institute report combining radiocarbon, craniometry and XRF for an early burial, while distinguishing Karasuk parallels from local traditions.

sources.title: Selin and colleagues, An Unusual Burial at Pyatiletka-1 Mound 6
sources.note: Multidisciplinary burial study using radiocarbon dates, pottery fabric, local clay, birch identification and cautious cultural comparison.

sources.title: Kozintsev, The Origin of the Karasuk People: Craniometric Evidence
sources.note: Twenty-four male cranial samples show internal and regional variation between Classic and Kamenniy Log associated groups.

sources.title: Jeong and colleagues, Bronze Age population dynamics and the rise of dairy pastoralism on the eastern Eurasian steppe
sources.note: Genome-wide evidence that sampled Karasuk-associated individuals were highly heterogeneous; material traditions are not genetic ethnic labels.

sources.title: Murphy and colleagues, Dental palaeopathological analysis of Eneolithic to Early Iron Age populations from the Minusinsk Basin
sources.note: Comparative study of calculus, caries, enamel stress and age patterns in 214 people, including Karasuk-associated remains.

sources.title: Exploring Complexity in Bronze Age Exchange Networks by Revisiting the Bronze Mirrors of Central Asia and China
sources.note: Peer-reviewed warning that wide distributions and technological connections form complex networks rather than a single migrating culture.

sources.title: Hsu and colleagues, Tracing the flows of copper and copper alloys in the Early Iron Age societies of the eastern Eurasian steppe
sources.note: University repository record for chemical and trace-element research distinguishing copper, alloy and finished-object circulation around Minusinsk.

sources.title: National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage, Korean Archaeological Dictionary: Karasuk culture
sources.note: Official heritage dictionary entry on rectangular semi-subterranean houses, hearth rows, hand-built pottery, graves and bronze objects.

sources.title: Korean Archaeological Dictionary mirror: Karasuk culture
sources.note: National heritage institute dictionary mirror used for pottery and occupation-deposit evidence without expanding its ethnic interpretations.

sources.title: Yale eHRAF Archaeology, Early Nomad or Karasuk tradition
sources.note: Comparative archaeological description explicitly treating related groups as independent and interacting rather than politically integrated.

sources.title: ICOMOS, Rock Art in Central Asia
sources.note: Heritage synthesis of Minusinsk Basin geography and the uncertainty of assigning rock-art styles to Karasuk, transitional or Scythian periods.

sources.title: Raman spectroscopy of coloring materials at the Boyary I rock-art site
sources.note: Institute study using Raman spectroscopy; a possible Karasuk date rests on style and remains explicitly tentative.

sources.title: Nesterov, The Beginning of Iron Metallurgy in East Asia
sources.note: Regional review distinguishing widespread Karasuk-type bronzes from later and uneven adoption of iron technologies.

sources.title: Millet in the Bronze Age Altai Mountains: discovery, progress and research prospects, npj Heritage Science
sources.note: Recent review of millet evidence, dental health and the limits of connecting pathology directly to cereal consumption.

sources.title: University of Oxford, New radiocarbon dates and review of Minusinsk Basin chronology
sources.note: University record identifying the directly dated Afanasievo, Okunevo, Andronovo, Karasuk and Tagar sequence used in chronology research.

sources.title: Karl Jettmar, The Karasuk Culture and its South-Eastern Affinities
sources.note: Digitized museum-journal study documenting early typological arguments from knives and warning how interpretations have changed since 1950.

sources.title: Lazaretov and colleagues, The Final Bronze Age in the Minusinsk Basin
sources.note: Institute study reclassifying 900 to 700 BCE burials and showing overlap between continuing Late Bronze Age and emerging Tagar traits.

sources.title: Slepchenko and colleagues, Trepanation in a Late Bronze Age individual from southern Siberia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed report of one healed cranial opening in a peripheral and culturally debated burial; evidence of survival, not a general medical system.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Late Bronze Age archaeological traditions, chiefly documented in the Minusinsk Basin; the atlas span is overbroad.

batchIdentityNotes: Preserve exact id karasuk-culture and treat it as an archaeological classification, never a state, nation, ethnicity or language.
The atlas polygon and 1500 to 500 BCE interval are explicit audit objects, not accepted historical borders or consensus periodization.
No predecessor or successor links are inferred: neighboring labels and Tagar transition do not establish one-to-one entity continuity.
No contemporaneous writing is securely attributed; visual motifs are not converted into a fabricated script sample.
